items.prompt: How many layers does the OSI reference model have?
rubric: The OSI model has 7 layers.
4 is the TCP/IP model layer count and 5 is a hybrid teaching model.

items.prompt: Which protocol translates a domain name such as example.com into an IP address?

options.label: DHCP
ARP
DNS
ICMP

rubric: DNS resolves names to IP addresses.
DHCP assigns addresses and ARP maps IP to MAC, often confused with name lookup.

items.prompt: What is the standard well-known port number for HTTPS?
rubric: HTTPS uses port 443 by default.
80 is HTTP, 22 is SSH, 53 is DNS.

items.prompt: Which device forwards packets between different networks based on IP addresses?

options.label: Network cable
Hub
Repeater
Router

rubric: Routers forward packets between networks using IP addresses.
Hubs and repeaters only relay signals within one network.

items.prompt: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?
rubric: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits.
128 is IPv6 and 48 is a MAC address length.

items.prompt: Which of the following are transport-layer protocols? Select all that apply.

options.label: TCP
UDP
HTTP
IP

rubric: TCP and UDP operate at the transport layer.
HTTP is application layer and IP is network layer.

items.prompt: A new technician is labelling a wiring closet. A colleague asks which address type is burned into a network interface card by its manufacturer and identifies it on the local link. Which one is it?

options.label: Domain name
MAC address
Port number
IP address

rubric: The MAC address is assigned to the NIC hardware.
IP addresses are configured logically and can change.

items.prompt: Why does TCP use a three-way handshake before sending data?

options.label: To encrypt the data with a shared key before any of it is sent
To establish a connection and agree on initial sequence numbers
To choose the fastest route across the network for the later segments
To look up the IP address of the destination host from its name

rubric: The handshake sets up a reliable connection and sequence numbers.
Encryption, name lookup and routing are handled by other mechanisms.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why live video calls often prefer UDP over TCP?

options.label: UDP encrypts the media stream, so calls stay private without extra setup
UDP guarantees every packet arrives in order, so video frames never glitch
Occasional lost packets are better than delays from retransmission
UDP needs no port numbers, so data reaches the right app without extra setup

rubric: UDP avoids retransmission delay, suiting real-time media.
UDP gives no delivery or ordering guarantees and does use ports.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a subnet mask?

options.label: To hide a device's IP address from other devices outside its own network
To limit the speed of traffic that leaves the network through the router
To assign a unique name to each host so people can reach it by name
To show which part of an IP address is network and which is host

rubric: The mask separates network bits from host bits.
It does not hide addresses, name hosts or limit speed.

items.prompt: Which describes the difference between a switch and a hub?

options.label: A switch connects different networks and routes by IP address; a hub only links devices within one network
A switch works with IP addresses only, ignoring MAC addresses; a hub works with MAC addresses
A switch sends frames only to the port of the destination MAC; a hub repeats them to all ports
A switch broadcasts every frame to all ports it has; a hub learns where each host is connected

rubric: Switches learn MAC addresses and forward selectively; hubs repeat to all ports.
Other options reverse roles or confuse switches with routers.

items.prompt: A host has IP address 192.168.1.20 with mask 255.255.255.0. Which address is on the same network?
rubric: The first three octets must match for a /24 network.
The others differ in the network portion.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe the TCP/IP layered approach? Select all that apply.

options.label: Every layer must be implemented by the same protocol
Application data skips the lower layers when sent locally
Each layer provides services to the layer above it
Layers let protocols be changed independently of each other

rubric: Layers serve the layer above and allow independent change.
Layers use different protocols and data still passes through all layers.

items.prompt: A user can open a website by its IP address but gets an error when typing its domain name. Other sites by IP also work. What does this most likely indicate?

options.label: A broken network cable
A DNS resolution problem
A wrong subnet mask on the device
A faulty switch port

rubric: Working IP access with failing names points to DNS.
A cable, mask or switch fault would break IP access too.

items.prompt: Why does TCP put sequence numbers in its segments?

options.label: So routers can pick the shortest path to the destination
So the sender can encrypt each segment with its own key
So the receiver can reorder segments and spot missing ones
So DNS can map the hostname to the right server address

rubric: Sequence numbers let the receiver order data and detect gaps for retransmission.
Routing, name lookup and encryption are separate mechanisms.

items.prompt: Why is UDP often chosen for live voice or video calls instead of TCP?

options.label: UDP packets are never lost on a local network, so no recovery is needed
UDP encrypts media by default, which TCP does not do
UDP gives each connection more bandwidth, so media streams arrive faster
A late packet is useless in real time, so resending it wastes time

rubric: Real-time media prefers timeliness over reliability, so retransmission delays do more harm than a small loss.
UDP does not guarantee delivery or encrypt, and loss can still occur.

items.prompt: What is the role of a default gateway for a host on a LAN?

options.label: It forwards packets bound for other networks for the host
It translates hostnames such as example.com into IP addresses
It hands out IP addresses to hosts that join the network
It filters frames between devices on the same switch

rubric: The default gateway is the next hop for destinations outside the local subnet.
Name translation is DNS and address assignment is DHCP.

items.prompt: At which layer of the TCP/IP model does IP operate?

options.label: Link layer
Application layer
Internet layer
Transport layer

rubric: IP addresses and routes packets between networks at the Internet layer.
Transport is TCP/UDP; link covers Ethernet and Wi-Fi.

items.prompt: How does a switch differ from a hub when a frame arrives?

options.label: A switch sends the frame to the port of the destination MAC; a hub repeats it to all ports
A hub builds a table of MAC addresses and sends the frame out one port, while a switch copies it to every port
A hub forwards frames by destination IP address between networks, while a switch uses TCP port numbers
A switch and a hub both send the frame only to the destination port, but a switch does it faster

rubric: Switches keep a MAC table and forward selectively; hubs repeat to every port.
The roles in the distractors are reversed or confused with routing.

items.prompt: Which of the following are things DNS does? Select all that apply.

options.label: Caches answers for a period set by the TTL
Resolves a hostname to an IP address
Encrypts traffic between client and server
Assigns IP addresses to new hosts

rubric: DNS resolves names and caches records according to TTL.
Address assignment is DHCP and encryption is handled by protocols such as TLS.

items.prompt: A user's laptop is connected and can load a website when she types its IP address, but typing the website's name gives a 'server not found' error. Other sites by IP also work. What does this most likely indicate?

options.label: The network cable is faulty, so the link drops intermittently
The laptop's subnet mask is wrong, so it cannot reach remote hosts
Name resolution is failing, for example an unreachable DNS server
The default gateway is down, so no traffic can leave the LAN

rubric: Access by IP works, so connectivity and routing are fine; only name lookup fails.
Gateway, cable or mask faults would also block access by IP.

items.prompt: How many usable host addresses does the subnet 192.168.10.0/24 provide?
rubric: A /24 has 256 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses, giving 254.
256 and 255 forget one or both reserved addresses.

items.prompt: A host has the address 10.0.5.20/24. Which address is on the same subnet as it?
rubric: A /24 fixes the first three octets, 10.0.5, so only 10.0.5.200 matches.
The others differ in a fixed octet.

items.prompt: You set up a web server that should accept HTTPS connections on its standard port. Which port do you open in the firewall?
rubric: HTTPS uses TCP port 443 by default.
80 is HTTP, 53 is DNS and 22 is SSH.

items.prompt: What is the prefix length for the subnet mask 255.255.255.192?
rubric: 192 is 11000000, which adds two bits to 24, giving /26.
/25 is mask 128 and /27 is mask 224 in the last octet.

items.prompt: You want to see each router hop between your PC and a remote server to find where packets stop. Which command do you run?

options.label: `traceroute example.com`
`nslookup example.com`
`ipconfig /release`
`arp -a`

rubric: traceroute lists the routers along the path.
nslookup tests DNS, arp -a shows the local MAC cache and release drops a DHCP lease.

items.prompt: A host is configured as 192.168.1.130/25. Which of these hosts can it reach directly, without going through a router? Select all that apply.
rubric: A /25 here covers 192.168.1.128 to 192.168.1.255, so .200 and .129 are local.
192.168.1.100 falls in the lower /25 and 192.168.2.130 is in a different network.

items.prompt: A PC has IP 192.168.1.15, mask 255.255.255.0 and gateway 192.168.2.1. It can ping the printer at 192.168.1.50 but cannot reach any internet site. The router's LAN interface is 192.168.1.1. What change should you make?

options.label: Set the gateway to 192.168.1.1, which is on the PC's own subnet
Set the mask to 255.255.0.0 so the gateway looks local
Change the DNS server, because the gateway is only used for names
Replace the switch port, since the printer ping proves nothing

rubric: The gateway must sit on the host's own subnet; 192.168.2.1 is not reachable, so off-network traffic fails.
Widening the mask or changing DNS does not give the PC a working next hop.

items.prompt: A host has the address `192.168.10.77/26`. What is its network address?
rubric: A /26 uses blocks of 64 addresses, so 77 falls in the block starting at 64.
Choosing .0 treats the subnet as a /24; .72 and .76 are arbitrary rounding.

items.prompt: How many usable host addresses does a `/27` subnet provide?
rubric: A /27 has 5 host bits: 32 addresses minus the network and broadcast addresses gives 30.
32 forgets the reserved addresses; 62 is the /26 answer.

items.prompt: Which address is in the same subnet as `10.0.5.130/25`?
rubric: The /25 containing .130 spans 10.0.5.128 to 10.0.5.255, so .200 is inside.
10.0.5.100 shares the first three octets but lies in the lower /25 half.

items.prompt: Host `172.16.4.20/22` sends a packet to `172.16.8.5`. What does the host do first?

options.label: Sends the frame to the gateway's MAC, keeping 172.16.8.5 as destination IP
Broadcasts the packet to its whole subnet so the destination can claim it
Sends an ARP request for 172.16.8.5 because both addresses start with 172.16
Queries DNS to learn which MAC address belongs to the address 172.16.8.5

rubric: A /22 here covers 172.16.4.0 to 172.16.7.255, so 172.16.8.5 is remote and goes via the default gateway.
ARPing for the remote IP assumes the first two octets decide locality; DNS maps names, not MACs.

items.prompt: A router has routes `10.0.0.0/8` via A, `10.1.0.0/16` via B, `10.1.2.0/24` via C, and a default route via D. Which next hop does it use for a packet to `10.1.2.9`?

options.label: C
D
A
B

rubric: Routers use the longest matching prefix, and /24 is the most specific match.
Picking A or B uses a less specific route; D is only used when nothing else matches.

items.prompt: A host can ping its default gateway but cannot open `example.com` in a browser. Which next checks apply a sensible DNS-versus-connectivity test? Select all that apply.

options.label: Check which DNS server addresses the host is configured to use
Ping a public IP address directly, such as 8.8.8.8
Change the subnet mask on the host to /8
Clear the MAC address table on the access switch
Run `nslookup example.com 8.8.8.8` to query a specific resolver

rubric: Pinging by IP separates routing problems from name resolution, and querying or inspecting resolvers isolates DNS.
Changing the mask or clearing the switch table does not address a name-resolution failure.

items.prompt: You are reading a packet capture of a new connection to a web server. The client sends a TCP SYN with sequence number 5000, and the server's port is open and accepting connections. You need to identify the next packet in the capture. Which packet should the server send?

options.label: FIN-ACK with acknowledgment number 5001
SYN-ACK with acknowledgment number 5000
SYN-ACK with acknowledgment number 5001
ACK with acknowledgment number 5000 and no SYN flag

rubric: The server replies SYN-ACK and acknowledges the next expected sequence number, 5001.
Acknowledging 5000 forgets that SYN consumes one sequence number; FIN-ACK would close, not open.

items.prompt: A host is configured as `10.0.0.5/24` with default gateway `10.0.1.1`. It reaches local hosts but nothing off-subnet. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The gateway address is outside the host's own subnet, so it cannot be reached directly
DNS cannot resolve names, so the host never learns where to send any packet bound off-subnet
The /24 mask is too small to hold any traffic that leaves the local network, so it drops it
The switch blocks the host from sending frames to any address ending in .1, including gateways

rubric: A gateway must be on the local subnet; 10.0.1.1 is outside 10.0.0.0/24, so the host cannot ARP for it.
DNS and mask size don't stop an IP-based packet from being forwarded to a valid on-link gateway.

items.prompt: `nslookup example.com 8.8.8.8` succeeds, but browsing by name fails while `ping 93.184.216.34` works. What does this most strongly indicate?

options.label: The default gateway is dropping all outbound traffic from this host
The host's subnet mask is wrong, so it misjudges which hosts are local
The TCP handshake is failing because of a mismatched sequence number
The host's configured DNS resolver is unreachable or misconfigured

rubric: Direct IP traffic and an explicit external resolver work, so the fault lies in the resolver the host is configured to use.
A dropping gateway or wrong mask would also break the ping and the query to 8.8.8.8.

items.prompt: Host A is `192.168.1.10/24` and host B is `192.168.2.10/24`. Both plug into the same unmanaged switch with no router, and they cannot ping each other. Why?

options.label: Each host sees the other as off-subnet and needs a gateway that is absent
The switch ports negotiated different speeds, so the link between the hosts cannot carry frames
A /24 mask is only valid on routed links, so the switch refuses to forward frames between those hosts
The hosts' MAC addresses fall in the same vendor range, so the switch treats them as duplicates and drops frames

rubric: Different subnets require a router; the switch forwards frames by MAC and does not route between IP subnets.
Being on the same physical switch does not put hosts in the same IP subnet.

items.prompt: Users on a LAN report connections to `192.168.1.50` dropping at random. On one machine, `arp -a` shows the MAC address for 192.168.1.50 changing between two values over a few minutes. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The router is applying longest prefix match to the wrong route entry for that host
The DNS server is returning different records for the same host name over time
Two devices are configured with the same IP address and are competing in ARP
The TCP window size is too small, so segments arrive out of order and stall

rubric: An IP alternating between two MACs signals an address conflict.
DNS, routing and window-size problems do not change the IP-to-MAC mapping in ARP.

items.prompt: Across a VPN, small pings and DNS lookups work, but large file transfers stall. Packets carry the Don't Fragment bit, and a firewall in the path blocks all ICMP. Which cause best explains it?

options.label: The DNS cache entry has expired, so each large transfer must wait on a fresh lookup that never completes
The tunnel MTU is smaller than the packets, and blocked ICMP hides the needed signal
The subnet mask is too long, so large packets exceed the host range of the destination network
UDP traffic is being prioritised over TCP by the firewall, so file transfers lose every queue contest

rubric: Oversized DF packets are dropped, and blocked ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages stop path MTU discovery.
Small packets work, which rules out mask and DNS problems; the issue depends on packet size.

items.prompt: A `traceroute` to a server shows normal replies for hops 1 to 4, then only `* * *` for every later hop. Which explanations are plausible? Select all that apply.

options.label: The return path from later hops lacks a route back to the source
Routers beyond hop 4 do not send ICMP time-exceeded messages
Hop 4 is certainly dropping all forwarded traffic
The destination is guaranteed to be powered off
A firewall after hop 4 drops the probe packets or their ICMP replies

rubric: Stars show missing replies, which can come from filtering, ICMP suppression or asymmetric routing.
Stars do not prove the destination is down or that hop 4 forwards nothing, since real traffic may still pass.

items.prompt: An office LAN uses `192.168.0.0/24` behind NAT. After a VPN to a partner is set up, staff can reach local printers but not the partner server at `192.168.0.50`. The partner's internal network also uses `192.168.0.0/24`. Which analysis explains the failure?

options.label: DNS caching returns a stale record, which sends requests to the wrong port
The VPN encrypts traffic, so the partner server cannot decode the NAT headers
The partner server is on a different VLAN, which forces a TCP reset
Hosts treat 192.168.0.50 as on-link, so traffic never reaches the VPN gateway

rubric: Overlapping subnets make each host think the destination is local, so it ARPs locally instead of using the gateway.
The failure is addressing and routing, not encryption, VLAN resets or DNS caching.

items.prompt: A host is configured as 192.168.10.130/25 with default gateway 192.168.10.1. It reaches 192.168.10.200 fine but cannot reach anything outside the subnet. What is the root cause?

options.label: The gateway lies outside the host's /25, so the host cannot ARP for it
The destination networks have no return route to this host's subnet, so replies never arrive back
The /25 mask is too small to hold this host address, so replies from remote hosts get dropped
The host's ARP cache is full, so it can only talk to neighbours it has already resolved

rubric: The gateway address is not on-link for the host, so off-subnet frames cannot be addressed to it.
Distractors blame the mask size, ARP capacity or return routes, which would not explain why only off-subnet traffic fails.

items.prompt: A DNS A record had a TTL of 86400. At 09:00 the admin changed its IP and set the TTL to 60. At 11:00 some users still reach the old server while others reach the new one. Why?

options.label: Resolvers that cached the record before 09:00 keep the old answer until its original 86400s TTL expires
The new 60s TTL applies retroactively, but some resolvers refresh at random intervals longer than that
Authoritative servers replicate the change slowly, so some queries are answered with the old record
Browsers always ignore DNS TTLs, so every client keeps the old address until it is restarted

rubric: A cached entry lives for the TTL it was cached with, so lowering the TTL later does not purge it.
Distractors assume retroactive TTLs, slow authoritative replication or universal browser behaviour.

items.prompt: Over a VPN tunnel with a 1400-byte path MTU, pings and small API calls work, but large downloads hang after the TCP handshake. Hosts send 1500-byte packets with DF set. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The receiver's advertised window drops to zero whenever a transfer exceeds a few kilobytes, so the sender stalls waiting for a window update
The VPN gateway rate-limits ICMP echo, so small pings pass while sustained TCP flows are throttled and stall after the handshake
Full-size packets are dropped and blocked ICMP fragmentation-needed messages stop the sender shrinking them
DNS returns different addresses for large downloads, so those connections go to a second host that completes the handshake but drops data

rubric: DF-marked packets above the path MTU are discarded, and PMTUD fails if the ICMP feedback is filtered.
Small packets work, which rules out the window, ICMP rate-limit and DNS explanations.

items.prompt: A traceroute to a server shows hop 5 as `* * *`, yet hops 6 to 9 respond normally and the final hop is the server. What is the most reasonable reading?

options.label: Hop 5 is a layer 2 switch, which means it must be dropping the probes that it sees
The link into hop 5 is down, so later replies come from cached results stored on router 4
Router 5 drops all transit packets, and later hops are answered over a backup path with the same TTLs
Router 5 forwards traffic but does not send, or rate-limits, TTL-exceeded messages, so it is not a fault

rubric: Later hops answering shows traffic passes hop 5; it just does not report TTL expiry.
Distractors treat the silent hop as a forwarding failure.

items.prompt: A TCP transfer across a 200 ms RTT link with 1% random packet loss reaches only a small fraction of link capacity, though the link is otherwise idle. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: Slow start never ends on high-latency links, so the window stays pinned at its initial value
The 1% loss corrupts the checksum of acknowledgements, so the sender waits a fixed 200 ms each time
Each loss is read as congestion, so the window is cut and regrows only about one segment per RTT
Loss forces retransmission of the whole file, so total data sent doubles and halves the effective rate

rubric: Congestion control cuts the window on loss and recovers slowly, which hurts most when RTT is large.
Distractors misdescribe retransmission, slow start and acknowledgement handling.

items.prompt: On a LAN, a server at 10.0.0.50 works for a few minutes, then established sessions to it reset, then recover. A new device was added yesterday. Which observations support a duplicate-IP conflict? Select all that apply.

options.label: DNS queries for the server's name return NXDOMAIN during each reset
Services on the server's second NIC, which has a different IP, stay stable throughout
Traceroute from clients shows packets looping between two routers until the TTL expires
The ARP entry for 10.0.0.50 on clients alternates between two different MAC addresses

rubric: Flip-flopping ARP entries and IP-specific instability are the signature of two hosts claiming one address.
Routing loops and NXDOMAIN point to other fault domains.

items.prompt: HQ workstations use 10.1.0.0/16, and some HQ hosts live in 10.1.8.0/24. A VPN links a partner site that also uses 10.1.8.0/24. The tunnel is up, but HQ users cannot reach the partner server 10.1.8.20. What is the cause?

options.label: The VPN encapsulates only private ranges above 10.2.0.0, so lower 10.x destinations are discarded at the tunnel
Overlapping RFC 1918 ranges make routers disable the VPN interface until one of the ranges is renumbered
The partner's /24 is more specific than HQ's /16, so HQ routers prefer the tunnel and the partner then drops it
10.1.8.20 falls inside HQ's own connected /16, so workstations ARP locally instead of sending it to the VPN gateway

rubric: Workstations treat the whole /16 as on-link, so overlapping addresses never reach the gateway.
Distractors invent tunnel range limits or automatic interface shutdowns.

items.prompt: A new VLAN must hold 480 hosts plus 20 infrastructure addresses, with no growth beyond that. The team wants one IPv4 subnet with the least wasted space. Which prefix best meets these criteria?
rubric: A /23 gives 510 usable addresses, enough for 500 with minimal waste.
A /24 is too small and a /22 wastes more space.

items.prompt: Thousands of sensors each send a temperature reading once per second to a collector. A reading older than a few seconds is worthless, and occasional loss is acceptable. Which transport choice best fits these criteria?

options.label: UDP, because a lost reading is superseded by the next and no connection state or retransmit delay is needed
TCP, because its connection state lets the collector detect sensor failure faster than any datagram design
UDP, because it encrypts datagrams by default, so readings stay confidential without extra setup
TCP, because guaranteed delivery ensures every reading arrives, and retransmitted old data is still useful

rubric: Stale data has no value, so UDP's lack of retransmission and per-sensor state is the better trade-off.
Distractors favour reliability that the criteria do not need, or credit UDP with encryption it lacks.

items.prompt: A small branch has one ISP uplink, three subnets behind one router, and changes layout about once a year. The criteria are simplicity and low maintenance; failover is not required. Which routing approach is best?

options.label: BGP with a private AS number, because it keeps routing tables smaller for any branch design
A static default route to the ISP, because with a single exit the route never needs to change
Per-host static routes on every workstation, because they avoid depending on the router's table
OSPF with the ISP, because dynamic protocols are always preferable regardless of topology size

rubric: With one exit and rare changes, a static default route is the simplest option that meets the criteria.
Dynamic protocols add overhead with no benefit here, and per-host routes multiply maintenance.

items.prompt: To speed up failover, an engineer proposes setting every DNS record's TTL to 30 seconds permanently. Criteria: fast failover for two critical services, and low resolver load and lookup latency for everything else. What is the best judgement?

options.label: Accept it, because shorter TTLs reduce lookup latency by keeping answers fresher in each resolver cache
Accept it, because TTLs only affect authoritative servers and have no effect on resolvers or clients
Reject it and use low TTLs only on the critical records, since long TTLs elsewhere cut query volume and latency
Reject it and set every TTL to 0, because zero guarantees all caches discard answers instantly everywhere

rubric: Low TTLs cost more queries and lookups, so apply them only where failover speed matters.
Distractors misunderstand how TTL affects resolver caching.

items.prompt: Two departments share one flat /22 and broadcast traffic is degrading performance. Policy: both must still reach a shared file server, with filtering between them. Which fix best meets these criteria?

options.label: Add more switches in a ring so broadcast frames take several paths and spread the load
Replace the access switches with hubs so collisions are shared and broadcasts get isolated
Split into two VLANs and subnets joined by a layer 3 device whose ACLs filter between them
Widen the mask to /16 so each host has a bigger address pool and sees fewer broadcasts

rubric: Separate broadcast domains joined by a router with ACLs reduce broadcasts and enforce policy.
Hubs, rings and wider masks make broadcast or filtering problems worse or unchanged.

items.prompt: A team argues, 'NAT makes our hosts secure, so we can skip firewall rules.' Which critiques of this argument are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: NAT prevents infected hosts from opening outbound connections, so firewall rules would only duplicate it
Static port forwards expose internal hosts directly, and nothing in NAT inspects what traffic they carry
NAT's blocking of unsolicited inbound traffic is a side effect of its state table, not a defined security policy
NAT encrypts the payload between hosts and the internet, so the argument holds only for plain-text protocols

rubric: NAT's protection is incidental and port forwards bypass it; explicit firewall policy is still needed.
NAT neither encrypts traffic nor restricts outbound connections.

items.prompt: A branch has a 50 Mbps satellite link with 200 ms RTT. A TCP backup tool achieves about 2.6 Mbps using default 64 KB windows. The tool cannot be changed and the budget excludes extra links. Which action best meets these criteria?

options.label: Buy a second 50 Mbps link, since throughput is limited by capacity rather than window size
Switch the tool to UDP so no acknowledgements are needed, with no code changes
Enable TCP window scaling and size buffers to at least the 1.25 MB bandwidth-delay product
Reduce the MTU to 576 bytes so each smaller packet crosses the satellite hop faster

rubric: Throughput is capped at window/RTT, so a window near the BDP lets TCP fill the link without changing the tool.
Distractors add cost, shrink packets or require changing the application.

items.prompt: A multiplayer game sends each player's position 30 times per second. Criteria: lowest perceived latency, tolerance of occasional loss, and no value in old positions. Which transport design best fits?

options.label: UDP with no sequence numbers, because reordered packets are harmless when updates arrive this frequently
TCP with Nagle's algorithm enabled, because batching small segments lowers latency for frequent updates
UDP with sequence numbers so stale packets are dropped, since a retransmitted old position only delays newer ones
TCP, because ordered delivery applies every position and retransmission hides any loss from players

rubric: Stale positions have no value, so UDP plus sequence-based discarding avoids head-of-line blocking and retransmission delay.
TCP distractors confuse reliability with low latency; the no-sequence option ignores that late packets can overwrite newer state.

items.prompt: A 1 Gbps path with 200 ms RTT transfers a file at about 2.6 Mbps using default 64 KB receive windows. A colleague says upgrading to a 10 Gbps link will fix it. Which critique is best?

options.label: Wrong: throughput is capped near window divided by RTT, so the window must approach the roughly 25 MB bandwidth-delay product
Wrong: the limit is DNS lookup latency per connection, so caching resolver results restores full line rate for transfers
Right: more link capacity raises the ceiling, since TCP throughput scales with raw bandwidth regardless of the RTT
Wrong: the limit is fragmentation, so enlarging the MTU to jumbo frames removes the cap at any RTT on the path

rubric: A single TCP flow cannot exceed window/RTT; 64 KB / 0.2 s is about 2.6 Mbps, so the window must match the BDP.
Distractors blame capacity, MTU or DNS rather than the window-RTT product.

items.prompt: A web service will move to a new IP. Its A record has a TTL of 86400 s. Criteria: nearly all clients see the cutover within about 5 minutes, and resolver load stays low long term. Which plan is best?

options.label: Switch the record now and lower the TTL to 300 s afterward, since the new TTL applies to cached answers immediately
Lower the TTL to 300 s at least 24 hours ahead, switch the record, then raise the TTL again once the service is stable
Keep the 86400 s TTL and restart the authoritative server after switching, since that purges caches in client resolvers
Lower the TTL to 300 s just before the switch, then change the record, since resolvers refresh when the TTL changes

rubric: Caches hold the old record for up to the old TTL, so the lowered TTL must be published at least one old TTL before cutover.
Distractors assume cached answers adopt a new TTL or can be purged from the authoritative side.

items.prompt: Two active-active stateful firewalls with no state synchronisation sit between a LAN and the internet. Outbound packets sometimes leave via firewall A while replies return via firewall B. What is the most significant risk?

options.label: Firewall B drops replies for flows it has no state entry for, causing intermittent, flow-dependent connection failures
TTL expires in transit, since each firewall decrements it twice when traffic crosses both devices on the path
Firewall A's connection table fills faster, since it must track both directions of every flow that crosses either device
Replies are delivered but unencrypted, because only the firewall that saw the SYN applies TLS inspection to a flow

rubric: A stateful firewall only passes return traffic matching a state entry it created, so asymmetric paths break flows.
Distractors invent table, TLS or TTL effects that asymmetry does not cause.

items.prompt: A manager says, 'Our NAT gateway makes a separate firewall unnecessary.' Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: NAT encrypts traffic between inside and outside hosts, but it cannot authenticate the remote peer, so a firewall must handle that authentication step
NAT hides internal addresses so inbound scans cannot reach hosts, meaning a firewall would add only redundancy and no new control over traffic
NAT blocks unsolicited inbound traffic only as a side effect of missing mappings and enforces no policy on outbound traffic
NAT inspects application payloads for threats, but it cannot track UDP flows, so a firewall is needed to cover that one protocol

rubric: NAT is address translation; its inbound blocking is incidental and gives no policy control over outbound traffic or port forwards.
Distractors credit NAT with encryption, payload inspection or real security value.

items.prompt: A proposal stretches one /24 VLAN across three sites over a WAN so hosts can keep their addresses. Which are valid criticisms of the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Hosts at different sites cannot share a subnet, because addresses within a /24 must be physically co-located
A layer 2 loop or spanning-tree event at one site can disrupt all sites, enlarging the failure domain
Traffic between nearby hosts may hairpin through a single default gateway at another site, adding latency
A /24 supports only 62 usable hosts, so three sites cannot all be addressed from that one subnet
Broadcast and unknown-unicast traffic floods across the WAN links, consuming bandwidth at every site

rubric: Stretched L2 extends broadcast and failure domains and causes gateway tromboning.
Subnets need no physical co-location, and a /24 has 254 usable hosts, not 62.

items.prompt: A site-to-site IPsec tunnel cuts the effective path MTU to about 1400 bytes. Users report small pages load but large downloads stall, and an upstream provider filters ICMP 'fragmentation needed'. Criteria: no changes on end hosts, TCP traffic must work, and no reliance on fragmentation. Which fix is best?

options.label: Lower the MTU on every end host to 1400 through group policy so they never send packets larger than the tunnel
Clear the DF bit at the tunnel endpoints so oversized packets are fragmented, avoiding reliance on the filtered ICMP
Raise the interface MTU on the tunnel endpoints to 9000 so larger frames carry the data without any fragmentation
Clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel endpoints so connections negotiate segments that fit within the 1400-byte path

rubric: MSS clamping at the tunnel makes TCP endpoints size segments correctly without host changes or fragmentation, bypassing the black-holed PMTUD.
Distractors break the criteria (host changes, fragmentation) or worsen the MTU mismatch.

items.prompt: Design addressing from 10.20.0.0/22 with no overlap: LANs of 200, 100 and 50 hosts, plus two point-to-point links. Which plan meets every requirement using minimally sized subnets?
rubric: A /24 holds 254 hosts, /25 holds 126, /26 holds 62, and /30 holds 2, so this plan fits the needs without overlap.
Distractors use a /25 for 200 hosts, a /26 for 100 hosts, or overlap 10.20.1.64/26 with 10.20.1.0/25.

items.prompt: Design DNS for a public site with two requirements: survive the complete loss of one DNS provider, and shift traffic away from a failed server within about 60 seconds. Which design meets both?

options.label: Delegate to two providers with synced zones, but keep a 24-hour TTL to cut resolver load and speed repeat lookups
Use two name servers at one provider in different regions, with health-checked records and a 30 s TTL on answers
Use one provider and rely on clients' resolvers retrying alternate servers, so no health checking is needed for failover
Delegate to name servers at two independent providers with synced zones, and use health-checked records with a 30 s TTL

rubric: Two independent providers remove the provider single point of failure; health checks with a short TTL give sub-minute failover.
Distractors keep one provider, use a long TTL, or omit health checks.

items.prompt: Design segmentation: 300 IoT sensors may only publish to an MQTT broker on TCP 8883, corporate users must read the broker's data, and sensors must never initiate connections to corporate hosts. Which design meets all of this?

options.label: Place sensors in their own subnet allowed to reach any destination on 8883, and block corporate access to the broker entirely
Place sensors in their own VLAN with full routing to the broker subnet, since VLAN separation already blocks corporate access
Place sensors, broker and corporate hosts in one subnet, and use host firewalls on the sensors to block outbound traffic
Place sensors in their own subnet permitting only sensor-to-broker TCP 8883, with the broker in a separate subnet corporate may reach

rubric: A dedicated sensor subnet with a single permitted flow to a separately reachable broker satisfies all three constraints.
Distractors share a subnet, rely on VLANs without filtering, or block the corporate read path.

items.prompt: A branch has two ISP links and no BGP. Outbound traffic must fail over to ISP-B when ISP-A's upstream is unreachable even though its local link stays up. Which design meets this?

options.label: Two default routes with ISP-A at lower administrative distance, so ISP-B takes over when the ISP-A interface goes down
A default route via ISP-A tied to a probe of a remote internet address and withdrawn on failure, plus a backup via ISP-B
Equal-cost default routes through both ISPs, so a failed upstream is bypassed because flows rehash onto the working ISP link
A default route via ISP-A with a short routing-protocol hello timer, so the gateway quickly detects loss of the upstream path

rubric: Route tracking with a remote probe detects upstream failure while the link is up and withdraws the primary route.
Distractors depend on interface-down events, blind load sharing, or hello timers that don't exist with a static ISP link.

items.prompt: A proposal gives DHCP redundancy by running two servers, each configured with the identical full pool 192.168.10.100-250 and no coordination between them. What is the design missing?

options.label: Different lease times on each server, since equal lease durations make both servers answer every client request
Static ARP entries for all clients, since two servers cannot learn client MAC addresses without them present
Pool splitting or failover synchronisation, so the servers cannot lease the same address to different clients
A relay agent on the servers' own subnet, since clients must reach both servers through a router to receive offers

rubric: Uncoordinated identical pools can issue duplicate addresses; scopes must be split or use a failover protocol.
Distractors invent relay, lease-time or ARP requirements that do not address duplicate leases.

items.prompt: A dual-stack IPv6 rollout is designed for an office network. Which elements must the design include to work correctly and safely? Select all that apply.

options.label: Firewall rules permitting required ICMPv6 types such as neighbor discovery and packet-too-big messages
Health checks on services published with AAAA records, since clients prefer IPv6 and broken paths cause delays
RA Guard or equivalent on access ports so rogue devices cannot advertise themselves as the default router
NAT66 at the edge, since IPv6 hosts without translation cannot be protected from unsolicited inbound connections
Router fragmentation of oversized packets, since IPv6 routers split packets to fit each link's MTU

rubric: ICMPv6 is essential for ND and PMTUD, rogue RAs are a real threat, and broken IPv6 paths hurt dual-stack users.
Protection comes from stateful filtering, not NAT66, and IPv6 routers do not fragment in transit.

items.prompt: Forty branch offices all use 192.168.1.0/24 and cannot renumber this quarter. Each branch must reach HQ servers, and HQ must reach a print server at each branch. Which design meets this?

options.label: Bridge every branch LAN to HQ over layer 2 tunnels so the shared subnet becomes one flat network reachable from all sites
Advertise 192.168.1.0/24 from every branch into HQ and let HQ routers choose the nearest branch by lowest metric each time
Enable proxy ARP on HQ routers so they answer for every branch host and forward frames to the correct branch office
Give each branch a unique /24 and 1:1 NAT it at the branch edge; HQ uses the mapped addresses until renumbering

rubric: Identical subnets are ambiguous to routing; 1:1 NAT gives each branch a distinct reachable address space without renumbering.
Distractors keep overlapping addresses reachable only by ambiguity, duplicate-IP bridging, or proxy ARP that can't distinguish hosts.
